  • temperature and critical pressure.
  • It is the point at which the distinction between liquid and gas phases disappears.

  • It has no distinct liquid or gas phase
  • But exhibits properties of both liquids and gases
  • o Like a gas, it can diffuse easily and fill a container
  • o Like a liquid, it can dissolve substances (like solutes or oils)

questions.question: Discuss the advantages and limitations of using alcohol and acetone in plant extraction methods, with suitable examples. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss the advantages and limitations of using alcohol and acetone in plant extraction
  • methods, with suitable examples.
  • [K/CO4]
  • Extraction can be defined as the separation of desired active compound/s from plant tissues
  • using specific solvents - Solvent extraction - Two common solvents used in herbal extraction
  • are – alcohol and acetone.
  • a) Alcohol - two common alcohols include ethanol and methanol.
  • Advantages - Polarity: Polar
  • Boiling Point: Ethanol ~78°C, Methanol ~65°C
  • Solubility: Soluble in water
  • Extracts a wide range of polar and semi-polar compounds: alkaloids, flavonoids, glycosides,
  • tannins, saponins, and phenolic compounds.
  • Ethanol is food- and pharma-safe, commonly used in tinctures and liquid extracts.
  • Methanol is more polar and often used in analytical research.
  • Limitations: extracts are toxic for consumption, selective solubility, loss of heat-sensitive
  • compounds, high purity grade ethanol is expensive, etc.
  • b) Acetone - a colourless, volatile, and flammable liquid.
  • Advantages:
  • •
  • •
  • •
  • •
  • •
  • •
  • Polarity: Medium-polar (semi-polar)
  • Boiling Point: ~56°C
  • Solubility: Miscible with water and many organic solvents.
  • Efficient in extracting flavonoids, terpenoids, and some alkaloids.
  • V olatile and evaporates easily, which aids in drying the extract.
  • Used mainly in lab-scale or preparative extractions.
  • Limitations: highly flammable and toxic if inhaled or ingested.
  • • Highly polar or non-polar phytochemicals (like sugars, proteins, and lipids) may not be
  • efficiently extracted.
  • •
  • •
  • Residual solvent problem
  • Evaporation and loss of volatiles.
